_status: Web simulation for the 'paths' slide (five doors). Fictional office, invented addresses: 10.x is a private range and 203.0.113.x, 198.51.100.x are documentation ranges that never belong to anyone. The door names, 'desk' (what it looks like at your desk) and 'it' (what IT does) and the summary table are the Module 1 deck's table, word for word; keep them in sync with the deck.
title: The RSSO office network and its five doors

steps.title: Your office on the internet
steps.text: Every device inside has a private address, like the office PC's 10.0.0.23. The **firewall** is the office's one front door to the internet, with one public address.

steps.title: A citizen opens the portal
steps.text: Her phone looks up the portal's name (DNS) and gets 203.0.113.10. Her request crosses the internet; the firewall lets web traffic through to the portal only, and the page comes back.

steps.title: The lock: HTTPS keeps it Secret
steps.text: With HTTPS the data travels encrypted. Anyone in between (the café Wi-Fi, an internet provider) sees scrambled bytes, not names and ID numbers.

steps.title: Every way in is also a way in for attackers
steps.text: Attackers use the same cables. Next: the five doors they use most, and how the office closes each one.

tracks.label: Door 1 · Phishing and stolen passwords
tracks.desk: A message rushing you to verify, open or pay

steps.title: A fake “password expiry” email
steps.text: The attacker sends Ben an email that looks like it comes from IT. It passes through the email service and lands in his inbox.

steps.title: Ben types his password on a fake page
steps.text: The link opens a look-alike login page. What Ben types goes straight to the attacker.

steps.title: The attacker logs in as Ben
steps.text: With the password alone, the attacker opens Ben's mailbox: payout emails, attachments, and a trusted address to send fake requests from.

verdict.text: Door open: Secret and Correct are at risk

steps.title: How long would a password last?
steps.text: Most password attacks are guessing at scale, using lists from earlier leaks. Pick a sample, never a real password.

steps.title: Close it: MFA and email filtering
steps.text: The filter stops most fake emails. If a password is still stolen, the login asks for a second factor the attacker does not have.

verdict.text: Door closed: a stolen password is not enough

tracks.label: Door 2 · Old systems and lapsed licences
tracks.desk: Warnings that updates or antivirus expired
tracks.it: Patch and renew on a schedule

steps.title: Out of support, out of date
steps.text: The firewall's software no longer gets security fixes, and the antivirus licence on the office PC lapsed months ago. Nobody noticed.

steps.title: A known flaw, found by automated scans
steps.text: Attackers scan the whole internet for systems with flaws that are already public. The office firewall answers.

steps.title: Data copied, then everything locked
steps.text: From inside, they copy the applicant data out, then run ransomware on the PC, the database and the always-connected backup.

verdict.text: Door open: Ready is gone, Secret too

steps.title: Close it: patch, renew, retire
steps.text: Supported software with this month's fixes turns the known exploit away. A renewed licence and an offline backup limit the damage if something still gets in.

tracks.label: Door 3 · Exposed websites
tracks.desk: Public pages that show more than they should

steps.title: A website with a weak spot
steps.text: The portal runs an add-on nobody updated, and its admin page is open to the whole internet with the vendor's default password.

steps.title: The attacker walks in through the admin page
steps.text: Automated tools try the default password on thousands of sites a day. It works here.

steps.title: Records copied, home page defaced
steps.text: The portal can read the database, so the attacker can too: every applicant's record goes out, and the home page now shows the attacker's message.

verdict.text: Door open: Secret, Correct and Ready all hit

steps.title: Close it: update, scan, close what is not used
steps.text: The add-on is updated, the admin page is reachable from the office only, and its default password is gone. A regular scan checks it stays that way.

tracks.label: Door 4 · Shared accounts
tracks.desk: One unit password on a sticky note
tracks.it: One account per person, with logs

steps.title: One login for everybody
steps.text: Five staff approve payouts with one shared login, “approvals”. A contractor who left two months ago still knows its password, and his VPN access was never removed.

steps.title: A payout changed from home
steps.text: The ex-contractor connects over the VPN and logs in as “approvals”. He changes one payout's e-wallet number to his own.

steps.title: Who did it? Nobody can tell
steps.text: The log only says “approvals”. Six people knew that password, so no one can prove who changed the payout.

verdict.text: Door open: Correct is broken, and no proof who did it

steps.title: Close it: one account each, leavers removed
steps.text: Everyone has their own login, so the log names a person. Accounts and VPN access end on a person's last day.

screen.title: Approval log
lines: One person, one name, every time.

tracks.label: Door 5 · Personal apps for official files
tracks.desk: Lists sent by personal email or chat
tracks.it: Approved tools that are easy to use

steps.title: Work on a personal phone
steps.text: Sol needs the beneficiary list at a community visit. The quickest way: a photo of the screen on her own phone.

steps.title: Shared in a group chat, then forwarded
steps.text: She sends it to the team's group chat. The chat company's servers are outside the office, and anyone in the group can forward it on.

verdict.text: Door open: Secret is gone and cannot be recalled

steps.title: Close it: office tools, managed phones
steps.text: Sol opens the list in the office's approved app on a managed phone: encrypted on the way, nothing saved on the device, and the office can wipe it if lost.
